title: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107)
hookLine: on his way to the lions he writes seven letters, the first to use the words the catholic church

lines: A PRISONER ON THE ROAD TO ROME.
cards: A prisoner is being marched across Asia toward Rome. He's chained to a squad of soldiers, and in one letter he calls them ten leopards, who only get worse the kinder he is to them.
At the end of the road, wild beasts wait in the arena. Along the way, churches send people to meet him, sit with him, bring news. And whenever he can, the prisoner writes letters back.
He's the bishop of Antioch, and his name is Ignatius.

teach.b: First, where he comes from. Antioch is the city where, Acts says, the disciples were first called Christians. Ignatius leads that church as its bishop.

In his letters' greetings he gives himself a second name: Theophorus, God-bearer. Second, the letter to Rome. The Christians there might have had friends with influence, people who could get a sentence changed.
Ignatius begs them not to try.

Don't be kind to me at the wrong time, he says; let me reach God. Then the line today's carry comes from: I am God's wheat, ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ.
A bishop who has broken the bread of the Eucharist for his people now pictures his own body as grain for that bread. Third, a word still on church signs.

teach.h: WHERE CHRIST IS, THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.
teach.b: To the Christians of Smyrna he writes: stay with your bishop, and just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church. Catholic is a Greek word meaning universal, whole.
Ignatius uses it for the whole Church, gathered around Christ, wherever it is. Fourth, what worried him most. Some teachers said Jesus only seemed to have a body, only seemed to suffer.
Ignatius pushes back again and again: Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly suffered and truly rose.
For a man about to suffer in his own body, that mattered.
His story is kept as a martyr's, not as a call to go looking for death, but as a picture of a life given away so completely that even its ending could become bread for others.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Ignatius of Antioch each year, name him in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and his letters appear in the Office of Readings.

o: a Greek title used only for Rome's bishop
the guard who chained Ignatius on the road
God-bearer, the name Ignatius gave himself

games.q: Ignatius of Antioch — tap the pairs.
p: the letter that names the catholic church

s: Ignatius traveled to Rome as a free man to visit the church
he went under guard, a condemned prisoner, to face the beasts.
Ignatius asked the Roman Christians to win his release
he begged them not to try.

games.q: you're a Christian in Rome with friends in high places. a letter arrives from a bishop on his way to the arena. what does he ask you to do?
o: use your friends to get him freed.
games.why: Ignatius begs the Romans not to interfere: let me reach God, he says. he wants to be God's wheat, made into pure bread.

practice: Say his line to yourself on an out-breath: I am God's wheat.
Then ask what is being ground in your life right now, a hard job, a long illness, a slow grief, and, without having to like it, what bread it might become, for you or someone else.
If you pray, offer it to God; if not, let the picture of wheat and bread rest in you.

wordCard.voice: Theophorus. The name Ignatius gave himself, meaning God-bearer, as he wrote letters on the road to the beasts in Rome. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the catholic church — katholikos means universal, whole. Ignatius, to the Smyrnaeans.

carryVoice: Your line: wheat of God. Ground down, and still becoming bread. Day seven hundred three.
